7 min read Just now -- Press enter or click to view image in full size Server side rendering solved our blank screen problem and handed us a sneakier one: pages that look ready but ignore your clicks. For years we shipped enormous client-side JavaScript bundles and hid the white screen behind a loading spinner. Then, to fix SEO and First Contentful Paint, the industry swung back to rendering HTML on the server. Users got a full screen instantly. And a new bottleneck appeared, one that is much harder to see in a demo and much harder to fix in production. We call it the hydration bottleneck, and it is the single reason frameworks like Next.js, Astro, and Qwik are competing so fiercely right now. Three architectures currently claim to solve it. They are not interchangeable, and picking the wrong one for your project type is an expensive mistake. Let’s look at how each one actually works under the hood, and where each one earns its place. Zombie Interfaces: What Hydration Really Costs Classic SSR is mechanically simple. The server queries the database, renders HTML, and sends it down. The user sees a complete page almost immediately. The catch is that everything on that page is dead. Buttons, forms, dropdowns, all of it is inert markup until the JavaScript bundle downloads, parses, executes, walks the entire DOM tree, rebuilds the component tree in memory, and attaches event listeners one by one. That revival process is hydration. The user experience failure mode is specific and infuriating: someone sees a button, clicks it, and nothing happens. The page is visually ready but interactively dead. Performance engineers call this gap the uncanny valley of web performance. A quick note on how to measure it, because most articles still cite outdated metrics here. Time to Interactive was removed from Lighthouse, and First Input Delay was retired from Core Web Vitals in favor of Interaction to Next Paint (INP). If you want to see your hydration tax in numbers today, watch Total Blocking Time in lab tests and INP in field data. Long hydration on mid-range mobile devices is one of the most common causes of a failing INP score. React itself took a first step against this in version 18 with streaming SSR and selective hydration: Suspense boundaries let the page hydrate in pieces, prioritizing whatever the user touches first. That helps, but it only reorders the work. The full component tree still ships to the browser and still executes. The three architectures below go further, each attacking a different part of the equation. 1. React Server Components: Ship Less Code React Server Components (RSC), which entered mainstream use through the Next.js App Router, change what crosses the network in the first place. Classic SSR renders every component to HTML on the server, then sends the JavaScript for all of those components anyway, because the client needs it to hydrate. RSC breaks that assumption. A server component’s source code and its heavy dependencies never reach the browser at all. One correction to a common misconception: RSC does not replace HTML with a JSON stream. On the initial load the server still sends fully rendered HTML, so first paint and SEO work exactly as before. Alongside it comes the RSC Payload, a compact serialized description of the component tree, which React uses to reconcile the UI and to render subsequent navigations without shipping component code. The 'use client' directive is where you draw the network boundary: everything below it is a client component that hydrates, everything above it stays on the server forever. // The heavy imports in this file never reach the browser. import { db } from '@/lib/db'; import { marked } from 'marked'; import InteractiveLikeButton from './LikeButton';export default async function BlogPost({ slug }) { const post = await db.posts.get(slug); const htmlContent = marked(post.content); return (

{post.title}

{/* Only this button's JavaScript ships and hydrates */}
); }The 2026 chapter of this story is Cache Components in Next.js 16, which made Partial Prerendering (PPR) the default rendering behavior. Every route now produces a static HTML shell that a CDN can serve instantly, with Suspense boundaries marking the dynamic holes. When a request comes in, the shell arrives immediately and the dynamic parts stream into the same response as they resolve on the server. React hydrates each boundary progressively as its chunk lands. Read that model again slowly: a static page with small dynamic regions streamed in. If it sounds familiar, hold that thought until the next section. 2. Islands Architecture: Hydrate Only What Matters Press enter or click to view image in full size Astro attacks the problem from the opposite default. Where React assumes everything is interactive unless proven otherwise, Astro assumes everything is static HTML unless you explicitly say otherwise. A fresh Astro page ships zero component JavaScript. The interactive parts you mark become islands in that static ocean, and the killer feature is that you control when each island hydrates: --- // Astro component, runs on the server import Header from '../components/Header.astro'; import ReactCarousel from '../components/ReactCarousel.jsx'; ---
client:load, client:idle, client:visible, and client:media give you a per-component hydration budget. A carousel below the fold costs nothing until the user actually scrolls to it. This is why content-heavy Astro sites post Lighthouse scores that application frameworks struggle to match. Astro 5 added the missing piece for dynamic content: Server Islands. A personalized region, say a “recommended for you” box or a logged-in user header, can be deferred on the server and streamed into an otherwise fully static, CDN-cached page. Static shell, dynamic holes. Sound familiar? PPR and Server Islands are two independent implementations of the same architectural conclusion. The project’s trajectory also removes the “is this framework safe to bet on” question. Cloudflare acquired Astro in January 2026 with the framework staying MIT-licensed, and Astro 6 shipped stable shortly after with a rebuilt dev server that finally unified development and production code paths. For content-driven work, this is currently the most confident recommendation in the ecosystem. 3. Resumability: Skip Hydration Entirely The Qwik framework’s answer is the most radical: hydration is not a cost to optimize, it is an architectural mistake to delete. Qwik’s insight is that hydration is fundamentally redundant work. The server already knew the component tree, the state, and where every listener belongs, then threw that knowledge away when it serialized plain HTML. The client rebuilds it all by re-executing the application. Qwik instead serializes that knowledge into the HTML itself: application state as JSON, listener locations as element attributes, the framework’s execution context embedded in the page. The browser does not replay the application. It resumes it, exactly where the server paused. To be precise rather than promotional: the initial payload is not literally zero. A tiny loader of roughly one kilobyte sets up a global event listener. When the user clicks, Qwik fetches only the few kilobytes needed for that specific interaction. In production it also uses speculative module fetching, pre-populating the browser cache in the background based on what the server rendered, so the code for a click is usually already local before the click happens. The property that actually matters is this: initial JavaScript stays constant no matter how large your application grows. That is a scaling curve no hydration-based framework can offer. The honest caveat belongs in the same paragraph. As of mid 2026, Qwik 2.0, a full rewrite of the core, is still in beta, and the ecosystem, component libraries, and hiring pool remain a fraction of React’s. Resumability is the most architecturally elegant answer on this list and the biggest organizational bet. The Quiet Convergence Before the decision framework, notice what just happened across all three sections. RSC with PPR produces a static shell with streamed dynamic regions. Astro produces a static page with hydrated or server-deferred islands. Qwik produces static HTML with lazily materialized interaction points. Three ecosystems, three vocabularies, one shared conclusion: the page is static by default, and interactivity is a scoped, explicitly declared exception. The real architectural question of this decade is no longer “SSR or CSR”. It is where you draw the boundary between server and client, and who pays to cross it. It is the same pattern I wrote about in the reactivity debate between Signals and the React Compiler: the frameworks disagree loudly about mechanisms while converging silently on principles. The Decision: Which Architecture for Which Project Press enter or click to view image in full size For SaaS products, user-specific dashboards, and applications with complex mutable state, React Server Components on Next.js is the pragmatic default. You get the ecosystem, the hiring pool, PPR’s static-shell speed, and a mature mental model for mixing server and client logic. The price is real complexity at the 'use client' boundary, and teams underestimate it. For content: blogs, documentation, marketing sites, news, and storefronts where most pages are the same for every visitor, Islands architecture wins outright. Astro’s zero-JS default plus Server Islands for the personalized corners covers ninety percent of what such sites need, at a fraction of the payload. For products where interaction latency on low-end mobile devices directly moves revenue, and where you can absorb ecosystem risk, Resumability is the ceiling of what is currently possible. Constant startup cost at any application size is a genuinely unique property. Just walk in knowing you are betting on the architecture before its ecosystem has fully arrived. Web performance is no longer about minifying what runs in the browser. It is about deciding what deserves to run there at all. So here is my question for the comments, and I want deployment stories, not benchmark links. If you run Next.js in production, has the client boundary stayed clean as your team grew, or is 'use client' slowly creeping up your component tree? And if you chose Astro or Qwik over React for a real product, what broke first: the tooling, or your assumptions?
